description:
We are a team of five third-year Data Science students participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, working on the “Be an Earth System Trend Detective” challenge.

Our team is interested in applying data science, statistical analysis, and data visualization to explore environmental changes using NASA’s Earth science data. We aim to identify meaningful trends, analyze their significance, and communicate our findings through a clear, data-driven solution.
summary:
EarthX is an interactive geospatial trend-detection tool for gridded climate time series. We analysed 45 years of monthly NASA observations (1981–2025) across three regions — the Mediterranean Basin, the Sahel and the Amazon Basin — on a 0.75° grid, testing four variables: precipitation, evapotranspiration, soil moisture and surface temperature.

Each grid cell is tested independently using the Hirsch-Slack modified seasonal Mann-Kendall test, with seasonal Sen’s slope for magnitude, confidence intervals for uncertainty, and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction for multiple testing. Every result receives one of three verdicts: Confirmed, Case Open, or No Evidence.

The challenge asks users to detect trends, so we made detection a guided investigation. Users predict before seeing data, examine one variable at a time, and build an evidence log that assembles into their own conclusion. For every Case Open result, we estimate how many additional years of observation would be needed to reach significance.

This matters because the two most common errors in reading climate data are mistaking variability for a trend, and reading “no evidence” as “no change”. EarthX makes both distinctions visible.
details:
EarthX is an interactive geospatial trend-detection tool with three case files: the Mediterranean Basin, the Sahel and the Amazon Basin. We analysed monthly NASA observations from 1980–2024 on a 0.75° grid for four variables — precipitation, evapotranspiration, soil moisture and surface temperature.

Every grid cell is tested independently with the Hirsch-Slack modified seasonal Mann-Kendall test, with seasonal Sen’s slope for magnitude, confidence intervals for uncertainty, and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction for multiple testing. Each result gets one of three verdicts: Confirmed, Case Open, or No Evidence.

The interface is an investigation, not a dashboard. The user predicts before seeing data, examines one variable at a time, and builds an evidence log that leads to their own conclusion — then compares it against the statistical verdict. Every Case Open result carries an estimate of how many more years of data it would need to reach significance.

Impact

The two most common errors in reading climate data are mistaking variability for trend, and reading “no evidence” as “no change”. EarthX makes both visible. The years-to-significance estimate turns uncertainty into something concrete: not yes or no, but not yet.

Tools

Python with [pandas/numpy/xarray] and [pymannkendall/statsmodels]. Data from [NASA products]. Frontend in [framework] with [map library] and [charting library]. Code public on GitHub under EarthXTeam.

Creativity

The tool withholds its conclusion so the user performs the detection themselves. The prediction prompt makes a wrong guess more instructive than a right one, and years-to-significance reframes an inconclusive result as a measurable distance from a verdict rather than a dead end.

What we considered

  • Our first candidate dataset’s documentation advises against using it for independent trend analysis, so we moved to NASA sources.
  • Non-parametric methods throughout, because monthly climate data isn’t normally distributed.
  • FDR correction, because thousands of tests guarantee false positives.
  • Our first JSON design embedded the full series in every cell — hundreds of MB per variable. We split it into a map file and a regional series file.
  • The frontend never interprets statistics; verdicts and plain-language text are computed upstream.
